items.definition: Known as the 'Mother of all communication models', this linear model includes information source, transmitter, channel, receiver, destination, and noise source.
items.rationalization: Developed by Claude Shannon and Warren Weaver in 1949 for telephone communication, it introduced the concept of 'noise' as any interference that disrupts message transmission.
items.tosCompetency: Analyze models and elements of communication processes

items.definition: A communication model identifying four key components: Source, Message, Channel, and Receiver, each influenced by specific behavioral factors like communication skills and culture.
items.rationalization: David Berlo emphasized that the sender and receiver must operate on similar wavelengths (attitude, knowledge, social system) for effective communication without distortion.
items.tosCompetency: Differentiate linear and interactive models of communication

items.definition: A cyclical communication model asserting that communication occurs only if there is an overlap in the 'Field of Experience' between encoder and decoder.
items.rationalization: Wilbur Schramm highlighted that shared background, language, beliefs, and culture (Field of Experience) are prerequisites for mutual understanding.
items.tosCompetency: Evaluate factors affecting intercultural and interpersonal communication

items.definition: A barrier to communication caused by ambiguous words, jargon, idioms, or differing interpretations of linguistic symbols.
items.rationalization: Unlike physical noise (loud engines) or physiological noise (deafness, headache), semantic noise stems from word meanings, specialized vocabulary, or grammatical ambiguity.
items.tosCompetency: Identify communication barriers and noise factors

items.definition: Prejudices, emotional biases, closed-mindedness, or anger that prevent a listener from objectively receiving a message.
items.rationalization: Internal psychological barriers such as anger, mistrust, stereotyping, or defensiveness distort message reception even in quiet physical environments.
items.tosCompetency: Identify communication barriers and noise factors

items.definition: Bodily conditions such as hearing impairment, hunger, extreme exhaustion, or headache that hinder communication processing.
items.rationalization: Physiological noise arises from the physical state of the human body, reducing the cognitive ability to encode or decode messages effectively.
items.tosCompetency: Classify types of communication noise

items.definition: The study of personal space and physical distance between individuals as an indicator of relationship and communicative intent.
items.rationalization: Edward T. Hall identified four spatial zones: Intimate (0-1.5 ft), Personal (1.5-4 ft), Social (4-12 ft), and Public (12+ ft).
items.tosCompetency: Distinguish non-verbal communication categories

items.definition: The study of body movement, facial expressions, eye contact, and gestures in non-verbal communication.
items.rationalization: Coined by Ray Birdwhistell, kinesics analyzes gestures (emblems, illustrators, affect displays, regulators, adaptors) communicating emotions and unspoken intentions.
items.tosCompetency: Distinguish non-verbal communication categories

items.definition: The study of the role of time in human communication, including punctuality, willingness to wait, and pacing of speech.
items.rationalization: Chronemics distinguishes between monochronic cultures (view time as linear, schedules strictly observed) and polychronic cultures (multitasking, fluid relationships take precedence).
items.tosCompetency: Differentiate cross-cultural temporal behaviors

items.definition: The study of touch as a form of non-verbal communication, expressing affection, sympathy, dominance, or greeting.
items.rationalization: Haptic behavior varies widely across cultures and social contexts (e.g., handshakes, pats on the back, hugging, or strict taboos against touching).
items.tosCompetency: Distinguish non-verbal communication categories

items.definition: Vocal qualities that accompany spoken language, including pitch, tone, volume, speed, pauses, and vocal inflections.
items.rationalization: Paralanguage conveys how something is said rather than what is said. Sarcasm, hesitation, or urgency are decoded through vocalic cues.

mnemonic.title: Paralanguage Rule
mnemonic.phrase: Not What You Say, But How You Say It

items.tosCompetency: Analyze paralanguage and vocal cues in speech

items.definition: A style of language that never changes, used in solemn ceremonies, the National Anthem, the Lord's Prayer, and the Constitution.
items.rationalization: Frozen register is historic, ceremonial, and immutable; listeners are not invited to alter the text or give casual conversational feedback.

mnemonic.title: Frozen Register Key
mnemonic.phrase: Frozen in Time, Cannot Rhyme Or Change

items.tosCompetency: Identify language registers according to communicative context

items.definition: Language used in professional, academic, or legal contexts where standard grammar, complete sentences, and respectful diction are required.
items.rationalization: Seen in scholarly papers, state addresses, graduation speeches, and corporate announcements; avoids slang and contractions.
items.tosCompetency: Identify language registers according to communicative context

items.definition: A two-way communication register used in professional exchanges like doctor-patient, teacher-student, or lawyer-client consultations.
items.rationalization: The speaker supplies background information while the listener continuously responds with verbal and non-verbal cues ('I see', 'Go on').
items.tosCompetency: Identify language registers according to communicative context

items.definition: Informal language shared among peers and friends, characterized by slang, colloquialisms, ellipses, and humor.
items.rationalization: Social intimacy without formality; friends talk in casual register using vernacular terms, idioms, and relaxed grammar.
items.tosCompetency: Identify language registers according to communicative context

items.definition: Private communication reserved for close family members, spouses, or best friends, featuring private codes, pet names, and non-verbal shorthand.
items.rationalization: Does not require complete grammatical clarity because intimate partners share extensive mutual understanding and private signals.

mnemonic.title: Intimate Register
items: N - No need for formal words

items.tosCompetency: Identify language registers according to communicative context

items.definition: The basic act of uttering meaningful words and producing sounds with determinate sense and reference (the literal utterance).
items.rationalization: Proposed by J.L. Austin in Speech Act Theory. Stating 'It is raining outside' literally states the weather condition as a locutionary act.
items.tosCompetency: Classify speech acts based on Austin and Searle

items.definition: The social function, intention, or communicative force behind an utterance (promising, commanding, warning, apologizing).
items.rationalization: When a speaker says 'There is a ferocious dog behind you', the illocutionary force is a warning rather than mere meteorology or biology.
items.tosCompetency: Classify speech acts based on Austin and Searle

items.definition: The resulting psychological effect, consequence, or behavioral response elicited in the listener by the speaker's utterance.
items.rationalization: If the listener gets scared and climbs a tree after hearing the warning, that fright and reaction constitute the perlocutionary effect.
items.tosCompetency: Classify speech acts based on Austin and Searle

items.definition: The tendency to judge another culture's practices and beliefs solely by the standards and values of one's own culture, viewing one's own as superior.
items.rationalization: Ethnocentrism creates acute intercultural friction; the remedy is cultural relativism—understanding practices from within their own cultural context.

mnemonic.title: Ethnocentrism Trap
mnemonic.phrase: My Culture is the Center of the Universe

items.tosCompetency: Examine intercultural communication challenges and cultural biases

items.definition: The principle of evaluating and understanding a culture's practices, beliefs, and behaviors through the lens of that culture rather than imposing foreign standards.
items.rationalization: Franz Boas promoted cultural relativism as essential for intercultural tolerance, ethical objectivity, and mutual respect in global communication.
items.tosCompetency: Examine intercultural communication challenges and cultural biases

items.definition: A communication style where most information is implied through relationships, non-verbal cues, and shared context rather than explicit spoken words.
items.rationalization: Prevalent in East Asian, Arab, and Filipino cultures (pakiramdaman, pahiwatig). Low-context cultures (USA, Germany) rely on explicit, direct words.

mnemonic.title: High vs Low Context
mnemonic.phrase: High = Hidden between lines; Low = Loud and direct

items.tosCompetency: Compare high-context and low-context cultural communication

items.definition: A balanced communication style expressing one's thoughts, feelings, and boundaries honestly and directly while respecting the rights of others.
items.rationalization: Distinct from aggressive communication (dominating/disrespectful) and passive communication (suppressing one's needs to avoid conflict).
items.tosCompetency: Select effective interpersonal communication strategies

items.definition: Listening to analyze, evaluate, and assess the logic, truthfulness, and credibility of a speaker's arguments before forming judgment.
items.rationalization: Essential when listening to debates, political campaigns, or advertisements to identify fallacies, emotional manipulation, and factual accuracy.
items.tosCompetency: Apply types of listening across varied situations

items.definition: Listening to understand another person's feelings, emotions, and perspective from their frame of reference without offering unsolicited judgment.
items.rationalization: Also called therapeutic listening; vital in counseling, conflict mediation, and building emotional trust between individuals.
items.tosCompetency: Apply types of listening across varied situations

items.definition: Listening for aesthetic pleasure, enjoyment, or inspiration, such as listening to music, poetry, theatre, or comedy.
items.rationalization: The primary purpose is personal satisfaction, relaxation, or cultural enjoyment rather than information retention or analytical critique.
items.tosCompetency: Apply types of listening across varied situations

items.definition: A speech delivered with thorough prior preparation, structured outline notes, and conversational spontaneity rather than word-for-word memorization.
items.rationalization: Preferred in professional and educational forums; strikes the balance between structured evidence and authentic audience engagement.
items.tosCompetency: Compare methods of speech delivery

items.definition: A speech delivered on the spot with zero advance preparation, relying on immediate quick thinking, knowledge, and structure.
items.rationalization: Often practiced in classroom exercises or ambush interviews; successful speakers use structures like PREP (Point, Reason, Example, Point).
items.tosCompetency: Compare methods of speech delivery

items.definition: A speech read word-for-word from a written text, used when exact wording and precision are critical (e.g., State of the Nation Address, legal declarations).
items.rationalization: Prevents misquoting or diplomatic missteps, but risks reducing eye contact and spontaneous connection with the audience.
items.tosCompetency: Compare methods of speech delivery

items.definition: A speech committed completely to memory and delivered without any script or notes.
items.rationalization: Allows maximum physical mobility and gesture use, but risks total disruption if the speaker suffers a memory lapse or mental block.

mnemonic.title: Memorized Trap
mnemonic.phrase: In the Head, Might Go Dead

items.tosCompetency: Compare methods of speech delivery

items.definition: Aristotle's rhetorical appeal based on the speaker's credibility, character, expertise, trustworthiness, and ethical authority.
items.rationalization: An audience accepts a message when they perceive the speaker as knowledgeable, virtuous, and of good will towards them.
items.tosCompetency: Apply Aristotelian rhetorical appeals in persuasive discourse

items.definition: Aristotle's rhetorical appeal to the audience's emotions, values, sympathy, desires, and passions.
items.rationalization: Effective persuasive speeches evoke empathy, hope, righteous anger, or pride to inspire action in the listener.
items.tosCompetency: Apply Aristotelian rhetorical appeals in persuasive discourse

items.definition: Aristotle's rhetorical appeal to reason, logic, sound evidence, statistics, syllogisms, and rational argument.
items.rationalization: Persuading through clarity of thought, undeniable facts, cause-and-effect reasoning, and deductive/inductive evidence.
items.tosCompetency: Apply Aristotelian rhetorical appeals in persuasive discourse

items.definition: A logical fallacy that attacks the opponent's personal character, appearance, or background rather than refuting their substantive argument.
items.rationalization: Latin for 'to the person'. Saying 'Do not believe her tax proposal because she is divorced' is an ad hominem fallacy.

mnemonic.title: Ad Hominem Meaning
mnemonic.phrase: Attack the Person, Not the Point

items.tosCompetency: Detect logical fallacies in reasoning and argumentation

items.definition: A logical fallacy of misrepresenting, exaggerating, or oversimplifying an opponent's argument to make it easier to attack and defeat.
items.rationalization: The arguer sets up a flimsy counterfeit argument (a straw dummy), destroys it, and claims victory over the real position.
items.tosCompetency: Detect logical fallacies in reasoning and argumentation

items.definition: The false cause fallacy claiming that because Event B occurred after Event A, Event A must be the cause of Event B.
items.rationalization: Latin for 'after this, therefore because of this'. Correlation or sequence in time does not prove causation.

mnemonic.title: Post Hoc Trap
mnemonic.phrase: After Does Not Equal Because Of

items.tosCompetency: Detect logical fallacies in reasoning and argumentation

items.definition: An appeal arguing that a claim must be true or good simply because the majority of people believe or do it.
items.rationalization: Truth and morality are not decided by popularity; widespread belief does not turn a falsehood into truth.
items.tosCompetency: Detect logical fallacies in reasoning and argumentation

items.definition: Introducing an irrelevant or sensational topic into a discussion to distract the audience from the real issue at hand.
items.rationalization: Named after dragging a strong-smelling smoked fish across a trail to confuse hunting hounds off the original scent.
items.tosCompetency: Detect logical fallacies in reasoning and argumentation

items.definition: Asserting that a relatively small initial step will inevitably trigger a chain of extreme and disastrous negative consequences without providing evidence.
items.rationalization: Assuming an extreme snowball effect without demonstrating the causal necessity between the stages.
items.tosCompetency: Detect logical fallacies in reasoning and argumentation

items.definition: The literal, explicit, dictionary definition of a word, devoid of emotional or cultural associations.
items.rationalization: The denotation of 'snake' is a limbless scaly reptile; contrast this with its negative connotation of betrayal or treachery.

mnemonic.title: Denotation vs Connotation
mnemonic.phrase: D = Dictionary definition; C = Cultural/emotional connotation

items.tosCompetency: Distinguish denotative and connotative meanings in text

items.definition: The secondary, figurative, emotional, or cultural association attached to a word beyond its literal dictionary meaning.
items.rationalization: Words like 'frugal' vs 'cheap' share the same core denotation (spending little money), but 'frugal' carries positive connotation while 'cheap' is negative.
items.tosCompetency: Distinguish denotative and connotative meanings in text

items.definition: The logical arrangement of ideas, sentences, and paragraphs so that the overall thesis and flow make sense to the reader.
items.rationalization: Coherence refers to the unity of thought and logical progression; cohesion refers to the grammatical and lexical ties linking sentences.

mnemonic.title: Coherence vs Cohesion
mnemonic.phrase: Coherence = Big Picture Sense; Cohesion = Sentence Glue

items.tosCompetency: Apply principles of effective paragraph writing

items.definition: The linguistic glue—using conjunctions, transitional words, and pronoun references—that physically links sentences together.
items.rationalization: Using transition markers like 'furthermore', 'on the other hand', and 'consequently' establishes clear cohesive ties.
items.tosCompetency: Apply principles of effective paragraph writing

items.definition: The author-date citation format predominantly used in psychology, education, and the social sciences (e.g., Smith, 2024).
items.rationalization: The American Psychological Association (APA) format emphasizes publication dates to reflect current scientific and educational research.
items.tosCompetency: Apply modern documentation styles and academic referencing

items.definition: The author-page citation format predominantly used in the humanities, literature, art, and cultural studies (e.g., Shakespeare 45).
items.rationalization: Modern Language Association (MLA) emphasizes authorship and exact page location rather than publication year.
items.tosCompetency: Apply modern documentation styles and academic referencing

items.definition: The study of eye behavior, eye contact, blink rates, and pupil dilation as a channel of non-verbal communication.
items.rationalization: Eye contact indicates attention, honesty, or dominance in Western cultures, while some Asian cultures consider direct eye contact disrespectful to elders.
items.tosCompetency: Distinguish non-verbal communication categories

items.definition: The non-verbal communication of taste, food sharing, and culinary gestures as symbols of hospitality, culture, and bonding.
items.rationalization: In Filipino culture, offering food to any house visitor ('Kain tayo!') serves as an immediate, warm welcoming gesture.
items.tosCompetency: Distinguish non-verbal communication categories

items.definition: The study of smell, body odor, and scent as a non-verbal medium of identity, status, and attraction.
items.rationalization: Aromas evoke strong emotional memories (Proustian memory) and influence first impressions and intercultural hygiene perceptions.
items.tosCompetency: Distinguish non-verbal communication categories

items.definition: The comma placed immediately before the coordinating conjunction (and, or) in a series of three or more items.
items.rationalization: Prevents confusing misreadings: 'I love my parents, Lady Gaga and Humpty Dumpty' without the serial comma suggests the parents are Lady Gaga and Humpty Dumpty.
items.tosCompetency: Apply punctuation conventions in formal written English

items.definition: Using the same grammatical pattern for two or more elements that have the same level of importance in a sentence.
items.rationalization: Example: 'She likes hiking, swimming, and biking' (correct) vs 'She likes hiking, to swim, and bikes' (faulty parallelism).
items.tosCompetency: Construct grammatically parallel sentences
